sections.heading: The 2026 landscape: who actually practices space law
paragraphs: Space law in the United States is practiced by two very different kinds of firm. At the top of the market, a handful of large firms run dedicated space and satellite practices inside their communications or aerospace groups. Chambers USA ranks the field nationally, and its 2026 guide puts Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and Milbank in Band 1, with Akin, Cooley, Greenberg Traurig, and Wiley in Band 2. Hogan Lovells Cadwalader is the product of the July 2026 merger between Hogan Lovells and Cadwalader, the largest law firm merger on record, and its space practice claims more than 200 space company and sovereign clients. Milbank's practice, led from Washington by Dara Panahy, is the finance and deals shop: satellite project financings, export credit agency debt, and M&A rather than routine licensing.

Below big law sits a small set of boutiques that live entirely on space work. Aegis Space Law, founded in 2020 in Washington DC, covers trade compliance, FAA launch and reentry, FCC telecommunications, NOAA remote sensing, government contracting, and company formation for startups, and holds a Chambers Band 3 ranking alongside Schroeder Law PLLC, a national security and commercial space boutique run by Franceska Schroeder. Solo practices matter here too: Ground Based Space Matters is run by Laura Montgomery, who spent over two decades at the FAA and managed its Space Law Branch.

There is now a third category on the map that did not exist when these practices were built: licensing platforms that execute the filings rather than advise on them. Invariant is the one built for space and nuclear: agents draft FAA, FCC, NOAA, ITU, and export control filings with every answer traced to the rule that requires it, and a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work through submission and regulator correspondence. It is not a law firm, which is exactly the point: most of a licensing program is execution, not legal advice, and the rest of this guide is about knowing which is which.

sections.heading: What space law firms do all day
paragraphs: The label covers four distinct businesses. Regulatory licensing is the one founders meet first: FCC space station and earth station authorizations, FAA Part 450 launch and reentry licenses, NOAA remote sensing licenses, and ITU coordination through the FCC. Transactions is where the large firms make their money: Pillsbury advised Stoke Space on funding rounds above $425 million and AT&T on its $155 million AST SpaceMobile investment, and Hogan Lovells guided SES through its $3.1 billion acquisition of Intelsat including FCC and national security approvals.

The third business is disputes and enforcement: satellite interference claims, export control enforcement, and formal FCC proceedings. The fourth is export control and government contracting: ITAR and EAR classification, DDTC registrations and licenses, CFIUS reviews, and FAR and DFARS compliance for companies selling to the government. Most firms are strong in one or two of these; almost none is strong in all four.

sections.heading: What space lawyers cost
paragraphs: Big law pricing is opaque but the market data is not. The 2025 CounselLink report found that the median partner rate at the 100 largest US firms crossed $1,000 per hour for the first time, with top-tier partners in high-value practices above $2,300, and regulatory and compliance partner rates growing 8.3 percent in a single year. A licensing project staffed with a partner and an associate at those rates accumulates cost quickly against a filing that may take a year to process.

Aegis Space Law is the rare firm that publishes prices. Its quarterly subscriptions run from $5,000 for about 12 hours of basic work (formation, trade compliance, contracts) to $44,000 for about 74 hours on the comprehensive plan that includes FCC, SEC, NOAA, and FAA licensing, with flat-rate projects and hourly billing offered alongside. One industry guide pegs total professional services for a first commercial small satellite license at $25,000 to $75,000, and $100,000 to $500,000 or more for a complex constellation, on top of FCC application fees. Treat those project figures as directional: they come from a single published estimate, not a survey.

sections.heading: What legally requires an attorney, and what does not
paragraphs: Less than most founders assume. No FCC rule requires an applicant to be represented by counsel: space station applications are prepared and filed electronically by the applicant, and the FCC's own form instructions require the application to be signed by the applicant itself, an officer or partner, with an attorney signing only in narrow circumstances such as the applicant's absence from the United States. University teams routinely file experimental satellite applications in house. The same holds for export control: DDTC registration is filed by the company through the DECCS portal, and ITAR license applications are signed by an Empowered Official, who by definition is a US person employed by the company, not outside counsel.

What genuinely calls for a licensed attorney is narrower and higher stakes. Privilege only attaches to communications with counsel, which matters the moment you are in an enforcement inquiry or weighing a voluntary disclosure to DDTC or BIS. Litigation and formal adjudications require bar admission. And relying on a legal interpretation as a defense, for example a commodity jurisdiction position or a novel reading of a licensing rule, is worth a lawyer's signature. The recurring work in between, preparing filings, tracing requirements, tracking deadlines, monitoring rule changes, is compliance operations, not the practice of law.

sections.heading: July 2026 changed the math: the FCC's Part 100 overhaul
paragraphs: On July 22, 2026 the FCC adopted a Report and Order (FCC 26-47) that discards the legacy Part 25 satellite licensing rules and rebuilds them from first principles as a new Part 100. The Commission describes the new regime as a licensing assembly line: applications are modularized, processed against bright-line public interest criteria, and pushed through a faster and more predictable pipeline. The order also revises surety bond requirements, license terms, and processing rounds, requires operators to share space situational awareness data, and opens a further rulemaking on a space-based experimental licensing regime. Law firm alerts note that default license terms extend from 15 to 20 years. As of early August 2026 the new rules are adopted but not yet codified: Part 25 remains the governing text in the eCFR while the transition lands, and the further notice is still open.

The strategic consequence for legal budgets: a certification-based regime rewards operators who can produce complete, internally consistent, well-cited applications quickly, and reduces the room for bespoke legal argument on routine filings. The scarce skill shifts from advocacy to execution: assembling the technical showings, keeping them consistent across FCC, NOAA, ITU, and export control workstreams, and staying current as the FNPRM and transition rules evolve. That is engineering and process work more than it is legal work.

sections.heading: Law firm, consultancy, or licensing platform
paragraphs: A working rule: hire a law firm for the things only a law firm can do. Enforcement defense, disputes, deals, privilege-sensitive questions, and genuinely novel interpretations belong with counsel, and the firms above are good at them. Consultancies fill gaps in technical analysis, spectrum engineering, and policy strategy. The recurring licensing pipeline, which is most of the work by volume, is a different problem: it rewards whoever can draft accurately, trace every answer to its source rule, and never miss a deadline or a rule change.

That is the problem Invariant is built for. Agents draft the filings, trace every requirement to the rule that created it, and monitor changes like the Part 100 transition as they land; a forward-deployed licensing engineer owns the work end to end, including submission packaging and regulator correspondence. Invariant is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice, and teams with counsel keep them for the questions that need privilege. What changes is where the hours go: the drafting grind stops being billed at partner rates.

faqs.question: Do I need a lawyer to file an FCC satellite license application?
faqs.answer: No. No FCC rule requires representation by counsel. Applications are filed electronically by the applicant, and the FCC's form instructions require the applicant itself, through an officer or partner, to sign, with attorney signature reserved for narrow cases such as absence from the United States. Many operators still use counsel or specialist help for complex commercial filings, but it is a choice, not a requirement.
